tldr: By layering a copper-powder silicone skin with circulating hot and cold water over a particle jamming layer that varies stiffness through particle confinement, the authors developed a desktop tactile interface that can independently and simultaneously modulate softness and surface temperature (10–50°C).
hero_caption: Overall system configuration of the proposed multimodal tactile display. In the user interaction section on the left, motor twisting of a fabric pouch controls particle stiffness, beneath a silicone skin embedded with fluid channels. In the control unit on the right, Peltier elements and a water-cooling block precisely regulate and circulate the water temperature.
overview:
When touching objects in VR or palpating tissue in surgical simulations, human skin simultaneously receives multiple sensory cues such as stiffness (softness), temperature, and texture. However, most conventional tactile displays could only present a single sensation—either a change in stiffness or a change in temperature. Combining them proved difficult because their physical properties interfered with each other: rigid thermal presentation modules degraded softness, while the large thermal capacity of compliant structures hindered temperature changes.

To solve this, the authors turned to constrained particle jamming, which adjusts particle stiffness purely via motor twisting torque without needing pneumatic pumps. They proposed layering a specialized ultra-thin silicone fluidic skin with enhanced thermal conductivity on top of this soft particle layer. By circulating heated or cooled water through this flexible skin, they achieved rapid surface temperature shifts without interfering with the underlying softness changes.

In validation experiments, the authors measured initial contact stiffness using an indentation tester and evaluated thermal characteristics using thermocouples and a thermal infrared camera. The results demonstrated that contact stiffness could be increased by up to 300% (from approximately 0.63 N/mm to 2.38 N/mm) depending on motor torque, while surface temperature could be stably controlled over a broad range from 10°C to 50°C.
contributions: Developed the first desktop tactile display capable of simultaneously modulating softness and temperature by combining pneumatic-free mechanical particle jamming with fluidic thermal transfer.

Proposed a multilayer skin structure that pairs a pure silicone insulating layer with a copper-powder composite silicone contact surface, optimizing thermal transfer without compromising the compliance of the jammed particles.

Demonstrated baseline performance by achieving an approximate 300% change in contact stiffness (0.63 N/mm to 2.38 N/mm) alongside surface temperature control from 10°C to 50°C (steady-state error of ±0.2°C).

sections.heading: Why VR and medicine demand simultaneous softness and warmth
sections.summary: Integrating temperature sensation alongside softness is essential for realistic touch perception. This section outlines the motivations and goals of combining particle jamming and thermal rendering—technologies previously developed in isolation.
sections.details:
Creating realistic haptic interactions in VR and medical training is rapidly growing in importance. In medical simulation especially, there is strong demand not only for the realistic elasticity of living tissue, but also for replicating localized fever or coolness caused by inflammation or vascular lesions.

Particle jamming has gained significant attention in soft robotics as a method for modulating softness. This technique transitions granular particles inside a container from a fluid-like state to a rigid solid in an instant by applying external compression to interlock them. Recently, methods generating confinement forces entirely through mechanical mechanisms—eliminating cumbersome pneumatic pumps—have emerged, facilitating device miniaturization and integration with other modalities.

Meanwhile, thermal sensations from skin temperature changes provide critical information directly linked to material identification, wetness perception, and affective haptics. While thermal displays use Peltier elements, fluid circulation, or infrared radiation, few attempts have been made to integrate them with variable-softness mechanisms. Placing rigid Peltier elements directly on the surface ruins compliance, whereas covering them with highly insulative soft materials prevents heat from reaching the fingertip.

This work aims to overcome these conflicting physical challenges by integrating a compliant fluidic thermal control skin onto mechanically constrained particle jamming, realizing a new multimodal tactile interface that simultaneously presents softness and temperature.

sections.heading: Hardware design combining torsional jamming and copper-powder silicone skin
sections.summary: Stiffness is controlled by twisting a 150 mm diameter circular particle pouch with a motor, topped with a fluid-circulating silicone skin mixed with copper powder. A circulation loop with a Peltier module and water block manages water temperature via a bang-bang/PID hybrid controller.
sections.details:
### 2.1 Softness
To control softness, the system uses constrained jamming. Twisting the edge of a fabric pouch applies radial compressive forces from all directions onto internal particles (quinoa seeds), stiffening the entire assembly. While earlier work used a square pouch that caused uneven stiffness between the center and corners, this prototype adopted a circular structure (150 mm diameter, 30 mm depth) to improve uniformity. The frame was 3D-printed in PLA using a Bambu Lab P1S. To handle the increased particle volume, a Maxon EC90 brushless DC motor with a maximum rated torque of 1.26 Nm and an EPOS4 controller were selected, enabling rapid, precise stiffness modulation via closed-loop current (torque) control.

### 2.2 Temperature
Thermal feedback is handled by an ultra-thin silicone skin attached to the top of the jamming container. The internal fluid channels were cast using Smooth-On Dragon Skin 10 FAST (a soft addition-cure silicone). For the top contact surface touched by the finger, the same silicone was blended with 325 $\mu$m copper powder at a 60:40 mass ratio. The copper powder significantly enhances thermal conduction across adjacent channels and between the circulating water and the finger. Meanwhile, the lower side of the channels (particle side) remains pure silicone, acting as an insulating layer that prevents heat loss into the high-heat-capacity particle bed.

To control water temperature, a custom closed-loop water-cooling system combines a 100 W Peltier module and a 40 mm × 40 mm copper water-cooling block. A CPU cooler (Cooler Master Hyper 212 EVO) and fan are attached to the heat-dissipating side of the Peltier. An Arduino Giga R1 WiFi runs a hybrid controller: bang-bang control delivers maximum power when the error exceeds ±5°C, switching to PID control within ±5°C of the target for stability. This approach mitigates integral windup caused by thermal transfer lag.

captions.F1: Overall system layout and channel geometry. The bottom-left inset shows the reverse side of the cast silicone skin, displaying the fine, concentric fluid channels.

sections.heading: Stiffness testing and thermal response setups simulating fingertip touch
sections.summary: To capture tactile sensation at initial fingertip touch, initial contact stiffness was measured over a low-force range (0.5–1 N). Thermal properties were evaluated by measuring heating/cooling limits, surface uniformity via thermal camera, and closed-loop response.
sections.details:
### 3.1 Softness
Particle jamming systems tend to locally compact and stiffen if deeply indented with high force. Furthermore, the presence of the soft silicone skin on top must be evaluated properly. Therefore, this study determined initial contact stiffness from the initial slope under light indentation forces (0.5–1 N), simulating a human fingertip lightly touching the surface.

The evaluation setup suspended a digital force gauge (Nidec-Shimpo FGV-1Z, 5 N capacity) from a linear stage, fitted with an 8 mm diameter flat-bottom cylindrical indenter (Fig. F2, left). Indentation tests up to 4 N were conducted on the surface while varying motor torque from 0 to 2 Nm in 0.2 Nm increments to measure stiffness and hysteresis (energy loss ratio during loading and unloading).

### 3.2 Temperature
To assess the temperature range, the Peltier module was first driven at maximum heating power (open loop) to circulate hot water, recording temperature every 0.25 seconds using a thermistor placed at the center of the top surface to find the maximum stable temperature. The Peltier polarity was then reversed at full cooling power to measure the lowest achievable temperature. Conducted in an ambient lab environment of 20.7°C, a thermal infrared camera (FLIR TG267, 120×160 resolution) visualized surface uniformity at extreme temperatures as well as heat leakage toward the jamming particles.

Additionally, closed-loop control was evaluated for practical usability. After heating to approximately 33°C, a step setpoint of 15°C was commanded to measure the time required to reach the target and the steady-state peak error.

captions.F2: Experimental setups. Left: initial contact stiffness measurement setup using a linear stage and force gauge. Right: surface temperature measurement using an attached thermistor and water-cooling unit.

sections.heading: Achieving a 300% stiffness increase and 10–50°C surface temperature control
sections.summary: Stiffness increased linearly up to 0.5 Nm of torque, reaching roughly 2.38 N/mm (nearly triple). The temperature spanned 10°C to 50°C, and closed-loop control maintained the setpoint with a tight ±0.2°C accuracy.
sections.details:
### 4.1 Softness response
In the softest (unjammed) state at zero motor torque, mean minimum stiffness was 0.63 N/mm with 84% hysteresis. Applying motor torque yielded a sharp, linear stiffness increase up to 0.5 Nm with a sensitivity of 0.00164 mm$^{-2}$, reaching 2.27 N/mm. Beyond that, increasing torque up to 1 Nm saturated stiffness at 2.38 N/mm. This represents an approximate 300% (roughly 3.8-fold) stiffness increase over the unjammed state.

Meanwhile, hysteresis decayed exponentially with increasing torque, dropping to just 2.1% at maximum torque. High hysteresis in the soft state stems from elastic energy stored in the indented silicone skin, but as the system stiffened, it displayed crisp, spring-like elastic rebound.

### 4.2 Thermal response
Under full-power heating, temperature rose with a time constant of $\tau = 290$ s, reaching a peak temperature of 50.2°C in 20 minutes. Full-power cooling yielded a time constant of $\tau = 325.5$ s, reaching a low of 9.3°C. Thermal imaging revealed highly uniform heating across the surface, with inter-channel temperature variations under 0.3°C. The inlet area was only slightly warmer by less than 2°C, confirming uniform warming across the contact pad.

Heat leakage into the underlying particle bed was minimal. Even when the surface exceeded 50°C, the pouch sidewall remained around 26°C; thermal images (Fig. F5 c) confirmed that heat remained concentrated in the fingertip contact layer.

In closed-loop testing, commanding a step from roughly 33°C to a 15°C setpoint reached the target in 12 minutes (average cooling rate of 1.5°C/min) and maintained the setpoint within ±0.2°C over the subsequent 15 minutes. However, an initial response delay of about 30 seconds occurred before the temperature began shifting.

captions.F3: Contact stiffness (blue) and hysteresis (red) versus motor torque. Stiffness rises sharply up to 0.5 Nm, accompanied by a rapid decline in hysteresis.
captions.F5: Thermal infrared images of the surface: top-down distributions at a) maximum temperature (~51°C) and b) minimum temperature (~11°C); c) side view during heating, showing minimal heat leakage to the side and concentration in the surface skin.

sections.heading: Multimodal tactile feasibility and dynamic response bottlenecks
sections.summary: While the prototype validated simultaneous stiffness and thermal feedback, slow thermal response (time constant ~5 minutes, 30 s latency) caused by fluid-system thermal inertia emerged as a key area for improvement.
sections.details:
The results prove that despite placing a soft silicone skin on top, the underlying particle jamming provides a substantial stiffness range (roughly 3-fold). Furthermore, stiffness tracked motor torque predictably and repeatably, making the device well-suited for stepped softness simulations.

Thermally, heating toward human body temperature proceeded smoothly, showing ample capability for simulating warm living tissue in medical training and affective haptics. The copper-powder composite silicone met design goals by aiding heat diffusion across channels to produce a uniform contact area.

On the other hand, slow thermal response was a clear bottleneck. Reaching extreme temperatures took around 20 minutes, with a 30-second lag before temperature shifts began. This lag is caused by natural heat dissipation from the relatively large 150 mm diameter pad, paired with the large thermal capacity (thermal inertia) of the Peltier module and fluid loop. While small temperature shifts reachable within 2 minutes can support material recognition tasks, the current setup cannot track rapid, dynamic VR transitions.

To overcome this, the authors suggest reducing contact area to boost thermal efficiency, or adopting a dual-reservoir system that routes pre-heated and pre-chilled water via valves rather than toggling a single Peltier between heating and cooling.

sections.heading: A stepping stone toward multisensory tactile rendering
sections.summary: This work proves particle jamming can serve as a platform reconciling physical conflicts across modalities. Future efforts will target faster dynamic response and explore perceptual studies and medical simulations.
sections.details:
This study demonstrates that particle jamming is more than just a variable-stiffness mechanism—it can serve as a robust platform for integrating disparate tactile modalities that normally conflict. Combining pump-free mechanical torsional jamming with a fluidic flexible skin enabled simultaneous stiffness and temperature control in a desktop-sized device.

Future work will focus on boosting thermal response speeds through improved fluidic designs. This interface can then be applied to cognitive science experiments investigating cross-modal interactions between softness and temperature on human perception (such as exploring Weber's illusion linking stiffness, temperature, and weight) and to realistic medical simulators for palpating vascular disease and tumors.

takeaways: Pairing mechanical torsional jamming with a compliant fluidic skin provides an effective architecture to deliver both stiffness and temperature without physical interference.

Using copper-powder composite silicone on the contact face and pure silicone on the underside achieves both heat transfer to the finger and thermal insulation from the particle bed without sacrificing flexibility.
Closed-loop control maintains high steady-state precision (±0.2°C), but thermal inertia across the fluid loop introduces latency (~30 s) and long time constants that bottleneck dynamic control.
limitations: Thermal response is slow, exhibiting a ~30-second delay before reacting and taking roughly 20 minutes to reach extreme temperatures, making it unsuitable for rapid dynamic interactions.
The relatively large 150 mm diameter surface leads to significant convective heat loss to the environment, degrading cooling and heating efficiency.
The study did not evaluate temperature recovery against external thermal disturbances (thermal robustness) or conduct psychophysical user studies to assess subjective human perception.
